title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Texas | Genstone
metaDescription: Texas investor renovations in Houston, Dallas, San Antonio, Fort Worth, Austin and El Paso: clay foundations, hail roofs, local permits and draws tied to work.
intro: Texas is really several renovation markets that happen to share a state line. Houston fights water from the Gulf, the sky and the soil. Dallas and Fort Worth sit on Blackland Prairie clay that cracks slabs and racks pier-and-beam floors, under a sky that drops hail on whole neighborhoods each spring. San Antonio and Austin layer historic districts, tree protections and new housing rules over older housing stock. El Paso is a high-desert brick city with flat roofs and swamp coolers. Genstone Construction plans and manages investor renovations in all six of those cities by coordinating vetted, licensed contractors who work there every day, while our estimators, field managers and billing team run the job from headquarters in Romeoville, Illinois. Every project starts with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that prices repairs and checks your ARV before you commit, then moves to a detailed scope with a draw schedule, one field manager, permits handled locally and draws released only against completed work.

sections.body:
Most investor renovation in Texas happens in three generations of housing. The first is the prewar core of each big city: Craftsman bungalows in the Houston Heights and Fort Worth's Fairmount, Tudor cottages in Dallas's M Streets and Oak Cliff, limestone and Victorian homes in San Antonio's King William, Hyde Park in Austin and brick bungalows in El Paso's Manhattan Heights. Outside El Paso, these houses almost always sit on pier-and-beam foundations, and they usually need leveling, rewiring, plumbing replacement and careful exterior repair.

The second generation is the postwar ranch, built in enormous numbers from the late 1940s through the 1970s. Brick veneer over slab-on-grade is the Texas standard, from Oak Forest in Houston to Lake Highlands in Dallas and Wedgwood in Fort Worth. Their weak points are buried: cast-iron drains under the slab, foundation movement on clay, small electrical panels and original ductwork.

The third generation is the tract subdivision of the 1970s onward, found on the edges of every metro and in suburbs like Katy, Pflugerville and Horizon City. These homes bring materials of their era, such as aluminum branch wiring in some, polybutylene supply lines in some and composite siding, and they make up much of the state's single-family rental inventory. Each generation needs a different scope, which is why a statewide template rarely fits a specific house.

Strategy in Texas follows the metro and, within each metro, the submarket. In Houston, inner-loop neighborhoods like the Heights and East End support character flips priced against new townhomes, while Sharpstown, Alief and the north side lean toward BRRRR and long-term holds, and flood history shapes every decision. In Dallas and Fort Worth, retail flips cluster in Lakewood, the M Streets, Fairmount and Arlington Heights, while southern Dallas, Pleasant Grove, the Northside and east Fort Worth suit rental investors who budget for foundation and roof work.

San Antonio's historic districts reward restoration-minded flippers, and the brick ranches near Joint Base San Antonio installations rent steadily to military and civilian households. Austin has shifted after its price correction: central flips still work on the right house, BRRRR has moved to Dove Springs, Montopolis and the suburbs, and the HOME rules have made added units a real option on many lots. El Paso's lower price points and demand from Fort Bliss, UTEP and the medical center make it a natural buy-and-hold market, with cooling conversions and flat roofs at the center of most scopes.

Across the state, small multifamily ranges from Tudor duplexes in Dallas to 1980s side-by-side duplexes in Austin and brick fourplexes in El Paso, and REO inventory is scattered through every metro. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built to sort out which strategy a specific house actually supports.

Texas does not issue a statewide general contractor license for residential remodeling, so the quality of a renovation depends heavily on who coordinates it and which trades they use. The trades themselves are licensed. Plumbers are licensed by the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners, and electricians and air conditioning and refrigeration contractors are licensed by the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation. Genstone uses licensed trades for that work on every project.

Building permits are issued locally. Houston has its Permitting Center, Dallas, Fort Worth, San Antonio and Austin each have a Development Services Department, and El Paso has its Planning and Inspections Department. Unincorporated areas fall under county offices, and many suburban subdivisions add homeowners association review. Local rules vary widely. Houston has no conventional zoning but enforces deed restrictions and floodplain rules. San Antonio, Fort Worth and Dallas run active historic preservation programs. Austin adds a tree ordinance, residential design standards, the HOME initiative and an energy audit requirement at sale for many older homes. Dallas requires rental registration. Along parts of the coast, the Texas Department of Insurance requires windstorm inspections for certain work, though that program does not cover most of the metros we serve. Because of that patchwork, we confirm the permitting office, district overlays and HOA rules for every address before a scope is final.

Texas weather shapes both what goes into a renovation and when the work can happen. Across Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, San Antonio and Austin, long hot summers dry out clay soils and drive foundation movement, push air conditioning systems to their limits and slow roofing, exterior paint and concrete work to early-morning hours. Spring brings hail and severe thunderstorms to North and Central Texas, and roofing crews get booked out after a major storm, so roof work is ideally scheduled ahead of that season when possible.

Central Texas sits in what is often called Flash Flood Alley, and Houston has a long record of major flooding from Allison, the Memorial Day and Tax Day floods and Harvey, so flood history and drainage deserve a look on any low-lying or creekside property. Hurricane season affects Houston directly and can tighten trade availability statewide. Winter is usually the most productive season, but Winter Storm Uri in 2021 burst pipes from El Paso to Houston, and the 2023 ice storm in Austin brought down tree limbs on roofs, so freeze protection is now part of every scope. El Paso adds its own pattern: intense sun, a summer monsoon that tests flat roofs and occasional hard freezes. We plan each project around its city's calendar.

faqs.q: Which Texas cities does Genstone work in?
faqs.a: We currently coordinate investor renovations in Houston, Dallas, San Antonio, Fort Worth, Austin and El Paso, along with surrounding suburbs and unincorporated areas in those metros. Genstone does not have local offices in Texas. Our estimators and field managers work from Romeoville, Illinois and coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in each market, with one field manager responsible for each project from start to finish.

faqs.q: Does Texas require a general contractor license for renovations?
faqs.a: Texas does not have a statewide general contractor license for residential remodeling. Plumbing, electrical and air conditioning work, however, must be done by trades licensed through the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners or the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation, and cities issue building permits and inspect the work. Genstone uses licensed trades for that work and handles permits, inspections and lien waivers on every project.

faqs.q: What are the most common rehab problems in Texas houses?
faqs.a: Foundation movement on expansive clay is the most common, followed by cast-iron drain lines under slabs, hail-damaged roofs, aging air conditioning and ductwork, and mixed or outdated wiring. Houston adds flood history and humidity, El Paso adds flat roofs and swamp coolers, and older homes everywhere need lead-safe practices. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices those items before you commit to a purchase.

faqs.q: How do payments and draws work on a Texas project?
faqs.a: Genstone does not take upfront payment. Construction draws are tied to completed work that you can verify through photos and milestone documentation, and final payment is due after completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris costs are included in estimates. Our work carries a one-year workmanship warranty that excludes tenant damage and normal wear, and lien waivers and contractor compliance documents are collected throughout the project.
